title: At the Landing
angle: Pauses are part of movement’s natural rhythm, not interruptions that need to be earned or explained.
paragraphs: At the top of a flight of stairs, people often pause for half a beat—not dramatically, just long enough to let the next decision arrive. The pause belongs to the climb as much as the steps do. Without it, ordinary movement can start to look like a test of uninterrupted effort.

We tend to picture motion as a straight line: start, continue, finish. Real days are less tidy. A walk pauses at a red light; gardening alternates between reaching and standing back; a game has a bench at the edge. These breaks don’t cancel the activity. They change its pace, and sometimes leave room to notice what it feels like.

Recovery can be understood not as a prize granted after enough exertion, or a failure when plans slow down, but as one of the conditions under which movement stays human. That doesn’t mean every pause is restorative or every busy day needs a lesson. Sometimes a chair is just a chair, which is useful.
The point isn’t to turn rest into another technique. It’s to leave room for a rhythm with more than one speed.
